name: Verna Felder
title: Verna Felder: Before the First Bell
dek: After more than twenty years in education, Verna Felder asks what happens before a family walks through the school door, and built a game so educators pause before judging.
excerpt: Verna Felder once had to choose between a tank of gas and a fifteen dollar field trip. Today she trains educators to look past the first explanation, and co-created Can You Survive Poverty? The Game™ to help.
seoDescription: Educator Verna Felder on poverty, schools and Detroit, and the game she co-created with Charlene Cutler so educators pause before judging families.
content:
A child misses school. An assignment goes unfinished. A parent's chair sits empty at a meeting. Verna Felder wants to know what happened before anyone walked through the door. After more than twenty years in education, as a teacher, a media specialist and a liaison supporting students and families experiencing homelessness, she has learned how much of a student's school day begins at home.

Some of that knowledge is her own. Raising three children as a single mother, she once had to choose between putting gas in the car and paying fifteen dollars for her daughter's field trip. She wanted to meet both needs and had to choose. Today, an unpaid fee is a reason to begin a conversation.

Four decks on the table

Those years shaped her book, Did You Bring a Bed Bug to School Today? How to Cultivate an Emotionally Safe Environment for Students in Urban Communities. They also led to her company, The Urban School Transformation LLC, and to Can You Survive Poverty? The Game™, which she created with Charlene Cutler.

The game puts four decks of cards on the table: Systemic Barrier, Support & Resource, Reflection Discussion and Life Event. Players navigate systemic barriers, unexpected life events and limited resources while trying to maintain stability, making decisions with what they actually have. The aim is to challenge the assumptions behind "Why don't they just...?" Felder is plain about its limits. No game can capture the full experience of living in poverty. What it can do is show how quickly circumstances narrow someone's options.

For her, the point reaches beyond empathy. She wants an educator to rethink an attendance response, and a leader to recognize when a process meant to help is difficult for families to access. "Understanding should change how we act," she says.

The signs staff cannot miss

Her work also reaches toward practical help: free eyeglasses, dental services, and partnerships with community organizations and service providers that put care within reach. A child struggling to follow a lesson may be unable to see the board. A student who seems distracted may be sitting through class with a toothache. A referral is only useful if a family knows what to do next, so she wants clear information, an accessible contact and someone willing to follow through.

That responsibility took on greater urgency when she learned that a school aged child had died while the family was sleeping in a car in a casino parking lot. It strengthened her determination to prepare staff to recognize distress early. A bus driver may notice persistent exhaustion. A cafeteria worker may recognize recurring hunger. An office employee may be the first person a parent tells about losing housing. Her trainings ask every adult to see the whole child, and to know what to ask and how to respond.

Farther than the block

In Detroit, she wants children's opportunities to reach farther than the blocks they grow up on. "Put a golf club in a child's hands. Take them to the opera," she says. When students meet successful professionals who look like them, she wants them to hear about the first application, the rejection and the mentor, so they can begin to map their own journey. A visit can become a mentorship. An interest can become a class, an apprenticeship or a business idea.

She believes in accountability, including meeting state standards, but wants it to reach everyone responsible for the conditions of success. Before asking why a classroom has fallen short, she asks whether it had a qualified teacher, appropriate resources and consistent support.

Her own standard comes down to three questions: Did I listen carefully? Did I follow through? Did anything improve because I became involved? Her advice to future leaders begins with another. "What would I do if I weren't afraid?" Then, she says, give yourself permission to act on the answer.

pullQuote.text: Your greatest testimony of growth may be the work you almost let fear talk you out of doing.
